meta.title: Who really said "News Is What Somebody Does Not Want You To Print. All the Rest Is Advertising"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Orwell never wrote it. Quote Investigator traces this newsroom adage to an unattributed 1918 placard; his name was first attached in 1999.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'News Is What Somebody Does Not Want You To Print. All the Rest Is Advertising'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Orwell. An anonymous newsroom adage documented from 1918; Hearst, Northcliffe and Muggeridge were credited first. Orwell's name arrived in 1999.

answer.label: Not George Orwell — an anonymous newsroom adage
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces this family of sayings to a little framed placard on a Chicago editor’s desk, reported in the New York trade weekly The Fourth Estate on 30 November 1918 — and already unattributed even then. This exact wording is documented in the London motoring weekly The Motor on 14 December 1937, credited only to an unnamed editor of a big-circulation newspaper. The earliest Orwell attribution QI finds is a January 1999 item in the New York Post, and in a different variant; QI calls the Orwell link “very weak” and labels the adage anonymous.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: An anonymous newspaper adage, documented from 1918
The Fourth Estate: A Newspaper for the Makers of Newspapers

source.excerpt: “Whatever a patron desires to get published is advertising; whatever he wants to keep out of the paper is news,” is the sentiment expressed in a little framed placard on the desk of L. E. Edwardson, day city editor of the Chicago Herald and Examiner.
trail: 1918 — The New York trade weekly The Fourth Estate reports a framed placard on a Chicago editor’s desk. It is the earliest strong match Quote Investigator ↗ has found, and it carries no attribution. By 1925 a Mississippi paper is already calling a version of it “the old saying.”

1937 — The London motoring weekly The Motor prints the compressed wording quoted today, putting it in the mouth of an unnamed editor of a big-circulation newspaper who used it to calm his directors after a big story. QI verified this citation with scans ↗.

1930–1988 — The famous names arrive: Walter Winchell gives it to Hearst, Jasper More gives it to Lord Northcliffe in the Commons, Malcolm Muggeridge gets the “public relations” rewrite, John Humphrys names Lord Rothermere. Barry Popik’s file ↗ tracks the same drift through American papers and calls the saying one of unknown authorship.

1999 — Orwell’s name is attached for the first time QI can document, in the New York Post. The Wikiquote page for Orwell does not list the line in either its Disputed or its Misattributed section, and The Independent’s fake-Orwell list ↗ states it cannot be found in any of his works.
source.excerptNote: The earliest strong match in Quote Investigator’s chronology — and already, in 1918, an unsigned motto on somebody’s desk rather than anyone’s coined line. The compressed wording people quote today (“News is what somebody does not want you to print. All the rest is advertising”) is documented nineteen years later in The Motor, again with no named author.
source.rightsNote: The line has no identified author, so there is no rightsholder to name. Its earliest documented ancestor — the unattributed placard text reported in The Fourth Estate on 30 November 1918 — is a pre-1931 American trade-paper item and would be out of copyright as printed, but that is a different sentence from the one quoted here. The exact popular wording is first documented in The Motor in December 1937 with no named author, so quotle.info asserts no copyright status for it.

author.name: L. E. Edwardson
author.heading: The desk the line was found on
author.metaLine: Day city editor, Chicago Herald and Examiner · earliest documented carrier of the adage, 1918
author.bio: Edwardson did not write this line. His desk is simply where it first surfaces in print. In November 1918 the New York trade weekly The Fourth Estate: A Newspaper for the Makers of Newspapers reported a little framed placard on the desk of L. E. Edwardson, day city editor of the Chicago Herald and Examiner, carrying what Quote Investigator ↗ calls the earliest strongly matching expression it has found. The item gave no attribution, and none has been established since — the placard was already repeating something the trade said to itself. Barry Popik, working the same ground, calls it flatly “an old newspaper saying of unknown authorship” ↗.

misattribution.heading: Six owners before Orwell
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually well-travelled saying. Before it reached George Orwell it had been credited, in print or in Parliament, to at least five other figures — and Quote Investigator ↗ finds documentary evidence for none of them originating it.

items.scope: The claim you will see today
items.why: The earliest Orwell attribution Quote Investigator documents is a January 1999 item in the New York Post, and in the “public relations” variant rather than this one. The Independent’s Top 10 fake George Orwell quotations ↗, guest-edited by Orwell Society trustee Benedict Cooper, lists it fourth and says its origin is unclear but it cannot be found in any of Orwell’s works. The Fallacy Files reaches the same verdict, classifying it apocryphal ↗.

Walter Winchell’s syndicated column ascribed a version to Hearst in 1930, and the British editor Brian R. Roberts credited him again in 1953 and 1955. Quote Investigator ↗ thinks it possible Hearst used the adage but finds no substantive evidence that he crafted it — and it was already in print, unattributed, twelve years before Winchell’s column.

The MP Jasper More credited Northcliffe with a near-identical wording in the Commons in 1968, and a Melbourne paper repeated the credit in 1976. Harmsworth did write, in 1903, that a politician’s business is to prevent certain news being printed — but that is a related observation, not this sentence, as QI’s chronology ↗ shows.

items.who: Malcolm Muggeridge, Lord Rothermere, Katharine Graham
items.why: Muggeridge was credited in 1979 with the “public relations” rewrite, John Humphrys attached it to Lord Rothermere in 1998, and a 2010 mediabistro list gave it to Katharine Graham. All are downstream repetitions in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗, decades after the saying was already in print.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion, based on current data, is that the adage is anonymous ↗ — a newsroom motto that was already unsigned when it first reached print in 1918.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Orwell
lead: The line is a piece of newsroom folk wisdom that has spent a century looking for an owner. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows it circulating as an unsigned motto in 1918, framed on an editor’s desk in Chicago, and being handed to a succession of press barons afterwards — Hearst in 1930, Northcliffe in 1968, Rothermere in 1998, Katharine Graham by 2010. Orwell was the last to arrive, in 1999, and by then the wording had already drifted from “advertising” to “public relations.”

It sticks because it sounds like him: terse, anti-cant, suspicious of official language. But Orwell put the thought differently and better, in a place that is documented. In his proposed preface to Animal Farm, first published in the Times Literary Supplement on 15 September 1972, he argued that liberty means “the right to tell people what they do not want to hear” ↗. That sentence is really his. The one on the mug is not.
detailsBody: The adage has no fixed text because it has no author to fix it. Quote Investigator records the 1918 form as a two-part contrast (“whatever a patron desires to get published is advertising; whatever he wants to keep out of the paper is news”), the compressed 1937 form that matches the popular wording here, and a 1979 mutation that swaps “advertising” for “public relations” under Malcolm Muggeridge’s name.

The Orwell version that circulates most widely today — “Journalism is printing what someone else does not want printed; everything else is public relations” — is that later public-relations branch, not the 1918 original. Some outlets that use it hedge it properly: Al Jazeera’s Investigative Unit prefaces it with “As George Orwell is said to have remarked” ↗.
context.pull: The saying was already anonymous in 1918 — a framed motto on a Chicago editor’s desk, credited to nobody.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest strongly matching expression is an unattributed framed placard on the desk of L. E. Edwardson, day city editor of the Chicago Herald and Examiner, reported in The Fourth Estate, 30 November 1918, p. 18 col. 4; the exact popular wording appears in The Motor, 14 December 1937, p. 917, credited to an unnamed editor of a big-circulation newspaper; Hearst (1930, Winchell), Northcliffe (1968, Jasper More), Muggeridge (1979), Rothermere (1998), Orwell (January 1999, New York Post) and Katharine Graham (2010) were all credited later; QI concludes the adage is anonymous and the Orwell linkage is 'very weak'.
Barry Popik's The Big Apple entry describes the saying as 'an old newspaper saying of unknown authorship' and collects newsroom citations from 1921 onward; it names no originator.

The Fallacy Files' 'Misquoting George Orwell' lists 'Journalism is printing what someone else does not want printed; everything else is public relations' (variant: 'News is something somebody doesn't want printed; all else is advertising') and types it 'Apocryphal', noting no citation to Orwell's writings is ever given and that the variant has been attributed to William Randolph Hearst.

The Independent's 'The Top 10 fake George Orwell quotations' by John Rentoul, guest-edited by Benedict Cooper, freelance journalist and trustee of the Orwell Society, lists this line at number 4 and says: 'Its origin is unclear, but it cannot be found in any of Orwell's works.'

The Orwell Foundation's text of 'The Freedom of the Press' contains 'If liberty means anything at all it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear', and its headnote states the piece is a proposed preface to Animal Farm, first published in the Times Literary Supplement on 15 September 1972 with an introduction by Sir Bernard Crick, and that the material remains under copyright.

The Al Jazeera Investigative Unit's 'Who we are' page uses the line with an explicit hedge: 'As George Orwell is said to have remarked, "Journalism is printing what someone else does not want printed; everything else is public relations."'
The Wikiquote page for George Orwell does not list this quote in any section, including Disputed and Misattributed (verified against the page's raw wikitext).
